1 
INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE 
Until 2017, no prisoner anywhere in the Nation had received a sexreassignment surgery while incarcerated. Over the past few years, however, States 
have faced a stream of lawsuits for refusing to provide surgeries and cross-sex 
hormones to prisoners who express psychological discomfort with the physical 
appearance of their bodies. Many courts have rejected those lawsuits. But other 
federal appellate and district courts have held that the Constitution requires States 
to provide sex-change surgeries and cross-sex hormones because the World 
Professional Association for Transgender Health (WPATH) and WPATH-aligned 
experts label those risky interventions “medically necessary.” See, e.g., Edmo v. 
Corizon, Inc., 935 F.3d 757, 796 (9th Cir. 2019).
The claims brought against the federal government in this case are little 
different from the claims that States have faced and continue to face. Here, as in 
other cases, plaintiffs argue that prison officials must follow WPATH 
recommendations and address gender dysphoria through cross-sex hormones and 
invasive sex-reassignment surgeries. Here, as in other cases, plaintiffs argue that 
there can be no real doubts about the safety and efficacy of their preferred 
interventions—notwithstanding a “robust and substantial good faith disagreement” 
within the medical community. Gibson v. Collier, 920 F.3d 212, 220 (5th Cir. 2019). 
And here, as in other cases, a federal court has invoked WPATH and WPATH-aligned 
experts to declare it “objectively unreasonable” for prison officials to side with medical 
professionals preferring non-invasive psychotherapy. App. 191a–193a.

2 
This Court should intervene to correct the error. Despite the insistence of 
WPATH and plaintiffs’ experts on surgeries and hormones, nothing in federal law 
requires the federal government or States to demand risky, controversial medical 
procedures of, at best, uncertain benefit to prisoners. And the law certainly does not 
appoint federal courts to be the referees of “fierce scientific and policy debates about 
the safety, efficacy, and propriety” of sex-reassignment procedures, especially in the 
prison setting. United States v. Skrmetti, 605 U.S. 495, 525 (2025). The Court should 
again make clear that authority to resolve those debates rests with politically 
accountable policymakers at the state and federal levels rather than a private 
advocacy organization or a district court’s preferred experts. 
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
As this Court has repeatedly emphasized, federal courts should be loath to 
countermand policy decisions that require evaluations of evolving medical evidence 
or that implicate prison management. The mere fact that the Administrative 
Procedure Act (APA) provides a path to reviewing the challenged Bureau of Prisons 
(BOP) policy does not authorize a district court to decide for itself what is the best 
way to care for prisoners with gender dysphoria. In this case, however, the district 
court improperly second-guessed considered policy judgments because it was 
persuaded by plaintiffs’ experts that sex-reassignment surgeries and cross-sex 
hormones are safe and effective. Its decision betrays a troubling tendency by federal 
courts to shut down legitimate debates by invoking expert opinion on one side—a

3 
tactic other federal courts have used in ordering States to provide sex-reassignment 
surgeries and cross-sex hormones to prisoners. 
Even if it were proper for federal courts to weigh the medical evidence for 
themselves, the challenged BOP policy is entirely reasonable. Study after study 
demonstrates that there is considerable uncertainty about whether attempting to 
alter someone’s physical appearance through surgeries and hormones to address 
discomfort with the person’s sex provides any lasting psychological benefit. Indeed, 
some studies suggest those interventions could contribute to worse mental health. 
The literature, meanwhile, makes clear that surgeries and hormones carry 
significant risks, even if one sets aside the very real possibility that prisoners who 
receive surgeries will later regret them. And even WPATH cannot confidently say 
that any study supports providing sex-reassignment surgeries to prisoners because 
no study of prisoners exists. Its insistence on surgery rests on a policy preference. 
Safety and security rationales independently support the challenged policy. 
Administering sex reassignment surgeries or cross-sex hormones exacerbates safety 
and security issues within the prison system. As States’ attempts to house prisoners 
show, housing transgender-identifying prisoners who look more like the opposite sex 
in either same-sex or opposite-sex prisons presents significant challenges. It can 
increase the risk of violence and harassment, compromise the privacy and religious 
convictions of other inmates, and consume prison resources. This Court should stay 
the district court’s injunction, making clear that federal and state policymakers 
should be the ones deciding how to manage gender dysphoria in prisons.

4 
ARGUMENT
This case sits at the intersection of two areas in which policymakers should 
have especially significant leeway—the regulation of medical interventions in an 
evolving area and the management of federal prisons. But the district court held it 
was “objectively unreasonable” and “implausible” to withhold sex-change surgeries 
and cross-sex hormones from prisoners who identify with the opposite sex. App. 191a–
192a (citation omitted). That ruling disregards the deference due to policymakers and 
accountable decisionmakers, defies fundamental principles of administrative law, 
and elides that no reliable evidence supports addressing gender dysphoria by giving 
prisoners surgeries and drugs to make their outward appearance more consistent 
with the opposite sex. And the district court’s ruling improperly discounts the 
challenges with prison management. 
I. The District Court Improperly Countermanded the Considered 
Judgment of Politically Accountable Policymakers 
Since the beginning of the Republic, policymakers have had broad authority 
over the regulation of medicine, especially in “areas where there is medical and 
scientific uncertainty.” United States v. Skrmetti, 605 U.S. 495, 524 (2025) (quoting 
Gonzales v. Carhart, 550 U.S. 124, 163 (2007)). That deference reflects that “the 
democratic branches are better suited to decide the proper balance between the 
uncertain risks and benefits of medical technology,” make value-laden judgments 
about the acceptable levels of risk, and weigh a procedure’s ethical implications.
Abigail All. for Better Access to Developmental Drugs v. von Eschenbach, 495 F.3d 
695, 713 (D.C. Cir. 2007); see FDA v. Am. Coll. of Obstetricians & Gynecologists, 592

5 
U.S. 990, 992 (2020) (“Our Constitution principally entrusts the safety and the health 
of the people to the politically accountable officials of the States to guard and 
protect.”) (internal quotation omitted); Marshall v. United States, 414 U.S. 417, 427 
(1974) (observing that the deference afforded to policymakers must be “especially 
broad” when they “act in areas fraught with medical and scientific uncertainties”). 
The need for deference is enhanced in the prison context. Prison 
administrators face an unenviable task. They are tasked with “trying to manage a 
volatile environment,” Sandin v. Conner, 515 U.S. 472, 482 (1995), while ensuring 
the health, safety, and security of prison inmates and staff alike. Because prison 
administrators “bear a significant responsibility for defining the legitimate goals of a 
corrections system and for determining the most appropriate means to accomplish 
them,” their “professional judgment” is “accord[ed] substantial deference” by the 
courts. Overton v. Bazzetta, 539 U.S. 126, 132 (2003). Even where a prison policy 
affects constitutional rights, any judicial inquiry is highly deferential. Id. (citing 
Turner v. Safley, 482 U.S. 78, 89 (1987)). The “operation of our correctional facilities 
is peculiarly the province of the Legislative and Executive Branches of our 
Government, not the Judicial.” Bell v. Wolfish, 441 U.S. 520, 548 (1979). 
In cases like this one, however, some lower federal courts appear to have 
forgotten their limited remit. Here, the BOP made a rational decision informed by a 
thorough review of scientific literature, the law, and state policies. The agency 
examined existing guidelines along with dozens of studies, clinical guidelines, journal 
articles, news articles, medical manuals, reports, care guides, declarations from

6 
medical professionals, and other medical resources. App. 19a–26a. That review 
included evidence showing that existing policies rested on guidelines from an 
organization that pursued “ideology, not science,” App. 31a, and that failed to 
consider the “special challenges of the inmate population,” App. 31a–33a. It also 
included independent systematic reviews of the medical literature that concluded no 
robust evidence supported using surgeries and hormones to address gender 
dysphoria, especially in women. App. 30a. And it included evidence that “hormonebased interventions for gender dysphoria are fraught with serious risks.” Id. 
Invoking declarations from experts that were not before the agency or were 
submitted after the BOP had formulated its policy, however, the district court held 
that it was “objectively unreasonable” to withhold sex-change surgeries and cross-sex 
hormones from prisoners with gender dysphoria. App. 191a–193a. But the 
Administrative Procedures Act (APA) does not authorize a court to decide which 
expert it thinks most persuasive or which set of prison policies would be best. The 
standard governing APA claims is “deferential.” FCC v. Prometheus Radio Project, 
592 U.S. 414, 423 (2021). It does not permit a court to “substitute its own policy 
judgment for that of the agency.” Id. Nor, for that matter, does the APA usually 
permit a court to entertain evidence postdating an agency policy. “[T]he focal point 
for judicial review should be the administrative record already in existence.” Camp 
v. Pitts, 411 U.S. 138, 142 (1973) (per curiam); see Dep’t of Com. v. New York, 588 U.S. 
752, 780 (2019) (“[A] court is ordinarily limited to evaluating the agency's 
contemporaneous explanation in light of the existing administrative record.”).

7 
As the federal government explains, these departures from fundamental 
principles of administrative law warrant a stay. See Stay Appl. 15–29. But they also 
betray a more fundamental problem with how a minority of federal courts are 
approaching cases involving transgender-identifying prisoners: invoking the opinions 
of WPATH and WPATH-aligned experts to “distort and stifle democratic debate 
under the guise of scientific judgment.” Skrmetti, 605 U.S. at 530–31 (Thomas, J., 
concurring). 
The Ninth Circuit’s decision in Edmo represents one of the most egregious 
(though certainly not only) examples of this tendency. In Edmo, the Ninth Circuit 
invoked WPATH’s “Standards of Care” to become the first court to mandate the 
provision of sex-change surgery to a transgender-identifying prisoner, holding that it 
would constitute “cruel and unusual punishment” to withhold the desired surgery. 
Edmo v. Corizon, 935 F.3d 757, 766–67 (9th Cir. 2019). Although Edmo arose under 
the Eighth Amendment, the Ninth Circuit’s decision bears many similarities to the 
district court’s decision in this case. There, as here, the court “substitute[d] the 
medical conclusions of federal judges” for that of politically accountable policymakers, 
allowed a “professional association” to “define what qualifies as . . . acceptable 
treatment of prisoners,” and disregarded an “ongoing medical debate” about how to 
address gender dysphoria in prisoners. Edmo v. Corizon, Inc., 949 F.3d 489, 490, 495, 
499 (9th Cir. 2020) (O’Scannlain, J., respecting the denial of rehearing en banc). 
Even at the time of Edmo—several years before recent revelations about 
WPATH’s pursuit of ideology over science and the emergence of further studies

8 
undermining its recommendations—there was a “sharply contested medical debate 
over sex reassignment surgery.” 949 F.3d at 497 (O’Scannlain, J., respecting the 
denial of rehearing en banc) (quoting Gibson v. Collier, 920 F.3d 212, 221 (5th Cir. 
2019)); see id. at 498–499. There was also evidence that WPATH had succumbed to 
“pressure” to be “an advocacy group.” Id. (quoting Kosilek v. Spencer, 774 F.3d 63, 78 
(1st Cir. 2014) (en banc)). Without evidence and “with the express purpose of 
influencing how courts review gender dysphoria treatments,” WPATH asserted that 
prisoners desiring sex-reassignment surgeries should not have to meet its usual 
screening criteria to receive them. Id. at 498. Yet the Ninth Circuit allowed WPATH 
to be the arbiter of what medical care for prisoners is warranted, just like the district 
court here. See Edmo, 935 F.3d at 796–97; App. 192a. 
Making clear that policymakers should have substantial leeway to weigh 
competing medical evidence and consider the unique challenges of the prison 
environment is critical if the courts are not to short-circuit legitimate democratic 
debate. Litigation against state policies that restrict cross-sex hormones and sexreassignment surgeries is pending across the country. See, e.g., Wagoner v. 
Winkelman, No. 25-6813 (9th Cir.); Allison v. Comm’r, Ind. Dep’t of Corrs., No. 
1:2024cv00577-RLY-CSW (S.D. Ind.); Robinson v. Labrador, No. 1:24-cv-00306-DCN 
(D. Idaho). Allowing the district court’s injunction against the BOP’s policy to stand 
would send the wrong message and all but ensure courts will continue to secondguess policymakers.

9 
II. No Reliable Evidence Supports Providing Sex-Reassignment 
Surgeries and Cross-Sex Hormones to Prisoners 
Even if it were appropriate for the district court to forage beyond the 
administrative record in evaluating the reasonableness of the BOP’s policy and 
evaluate the medical evidence for itself, the evidence does not support its view that 
“decades of research and clinical experience demonstrat[es] the efficacy of gender 
affirming care.” App. 192a–193a. In fact, there are “fierce scientific and policy debates 
about the safety, efficacy, and propriety” of these interventions. Skrmetti, 605 U.S. at 
525; see Clark v. Valletta, 157 F.4th 201, 213 (2d Cir. 2025) (recognizing that the 
First, Fifth, Eighth, Tenth, and Eleventh Circuits have “rejected deliberateindifference claims for denial of specific gender-dysphoria treatments”); Gibson, 920 
F.3d at 220 (observing a “robust and substantial good faith disagreement divid[es]” 
the medical community over surgeries); Kosilek, 774 F.3d at 76 (noting testimony 
from Johns Hopkins physicians that there are “many people in the country who 
disagree with” WPATH’s surgical recommendations). 
A. No reliable evidence supports surgeries and hormones 
Consider a few examples. In 2016, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid 
Services reviewed studies considering the effectiveness of sex-change surgeries.1 Of 
the hundreds of sources reviewed and cited, only six provided useful information 
regarding surgery. The four best-designed of those six studies “did not demonstrate 
clinically significant changes or differences in psychometric test results after” 
1 Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, Gender Dysphoria and Gender Reassignment 
Surgery: National Coverage Analysis Decision Memo, (Aug. 30, 2016), https://www.cms.gov/medicarecoverage-database/view/ncacal-decision-memo.aspx?proposed=N&NCA Id=282.

10 
surgery.2 A few years later, authors who set out to prove that surgery provides 
mental-health benefits were forced to retract their study after a reanalysis of their 
data showed “no advantage of surgery.”3 What is more, the authors affirmatively 
conceded that there is “a lack of sufficient knowledge to provide evidence-based 
treatment recommendations” for gender dysphoria.4 The effect of sex-reassignment 
surgery, they admitted, on “long-term mental health is largely unknown.”5
Similar concessions are found throughout the medical and scientific literature. 
A 2025 study concluded that those who undergo sex-change surgeries “are at 
significantly higher risk for adverse mental health outcomes, including depression, 
anxiety, suicidal ideation, and substance use disorder, compared to those who do not 
undergo gender-affirming surgery.”6 “This trend persists even after controlling for 
confounding factors.”7 Other researchers have published similar findings. One study 
reported that surgery has “not been shown to reduce even suicidal ideation.”8 A 2011 
study of all persons in Sweden who had received surgery over 30 years even reported

that trans-identifying patients remained suicidal after surgery at a much higher 
rate—19.1 times higher—than a control population.9 That study “found substantially 
higher rates of overall mortality, death from cardiovascular disease and suicide, 
suicide attempts, and psychiatric hospitalizations in sex-reassigned transsexual 
individuals compared to a healthy control population.”10
Even literature claiming psychological benefits reveals uncertain results. One 
Brazilian study assessed 47 transgender females at least one year before and after 
genital surgery. It found that psychological state and relationships improved, but 
physical health and independence deteriorated.11 Past the one-year mark,

regressed to the preoperative level by the five-year mark.13

B. Surgeries and hormones carry significant risks 
Though the putative benefits of sex-reassignment surgery and cross-sex 
hormones are, at best, uncertain, the dangers are quite real. Many of those who 
undergo vaginoplasties face complications such as flap necrosis, rectal and urethral 
injuries, rectal fistula, vaginal stenosis, and urethral fistula.22 Further, a review of 
17 studies following vaginoplasties found high rates of pelvic floor dysfunction: a 1-
7.5% rate of pelvic floor prolapse; up to a 15% rate of urinary incontinence; a 25-75% 
rate of sexual dysfunction; and up to a 20% rate of urinary irritation.23 Another study 
of 330 patients found a complication rate of 28.9% and a reoperation rate of 9%.24
Others have found complication and reoperation rates even higher, including one that 
found a complication rate of 32.5% and reoperation rate of 21.7%.25 A meta-analysis 
of 46 studies found an average complication rate of 21%.26 
The administration of cross-sex hormones also carries serious risks. Males who

III. The Provision of Sex-Reassignment Surgery and Cross-Sex Hormones 
to Prisoners Presents Significant Safety and Security Risks
In enjoining the BOP policy, the district court gave scant attention to unique 
challenges that sex-reassignment surgeries and hormones pose in the prison setting. 
As States’ experience shows, however, those challenges are real. Housing 
transgender-identifying individuals in prison can be an “intractable problem.” Bell, 
441 U.S. at 562. “Recognizing that reasonable concerns would arise regarding a 
postoperative, male-to-female transsexual being housed with male prisoners takes no 
great stretch of the imagination.” Kosilek, 774 F.3d at 93 (en banc). The same goes for 
housing inmates who take cross-sex hormones. It takes no leap for experienced prison 
officials to conclude that a male who appears more female will “inevitably become a 
target for abuse in an all-male prison.” Keohane v. Fla. Dep’t of Corr. Sec’y, 952 F.3d 
1257, 1275 (11th Cir. 2020). 
The only way to prevent disorder and ensure the safety of a male inmate who 
undergoes procedures to create a more feminine appearance may be to house the 
inmate “in a segregated protective custody unit.” Kosilek, 774 F.3d at 93. But that 
would require a substantial expenditure of resources for the duration of the inmate’s 
incarceration, and if the federal government or a State were to take that step, it could 
face claims that “such isolation would amount to a form of extrajudicial punishment 
that is prohibited by the Eighth Amendment.” Id. (internal quotation omitted). 
Requiring prison officials to provide sex-reassignment surgeries and cross-sex 
hormones while also keeping prison inmates safe just invites further judicial

micromanagement of problems uniquely within the expertise of executive and 
legislative branch officials. 
Housing transgender inmates with the opposite sex presents even worse 
problems. Those problems redound to the harm of female inmates who (1) have their 
rights to privacy and dignity compromised by having to sleep and shower with men, 
(2) are exposed to elevated possibilities of violence or sexual assault, and (3) could be 
pressured or coerced into using speech reflecting a belief that conflicts with biological 
reality. See App. 29a, 54a–55a. Indeed, instances of sexual violence have been 
reported in at least six States where transgender-identifying prison inmates are 
sometimes housed in opposite-sex prisons: California,42 Illinois,43 Maine,44 New 
Jersey,45 Oregon,46 and Washington.47 Transgender-identifying prisoners in the 
United Kingdom and Canada have also been charged with sexual assault after being
